lines.say: Here's a puzzle. Can a gate change a qubit, yet leave every measurement the same?
Picture the qubit as an arrow. Up always reads zero, and down always reads one.
The odds depend only on how far up or down it points, like latitude on a globe.
Cities on one line of latitude are equally far north, however far east or west they are.
That's longitude. Our arrow has one too, the way it faces around the globe, called the phase.
The Z gate spins the arrow half way round its line of latitude, so the odds stay put.
S turns it a quarter of the way, and T an eighth of the way.
Let's test it. Lay the arrow on the equator pointing right: fifty fifty.
Apply Z, and it swings round to point left. Still fifty fifty.
So did Z do nothing? The bars never moved, but the arrow turned.
Now add an H gate. It tips the arrow up or down, by which way it faces.
Without the Z, it lands straight up, and reads zero every time.
With the Z, it lands straight down, and reads one every time.
Same odds before, opposite answers after. The phase was there all along.
Here the globe breaks: maps print longitude, but phase can't be read directly.
Only a later gate can turn it into odds, a trick called interference.
In the formula, theta tracks latitude, setting the odds, and phi tracks longitude, the phase.
So phase is the arrow's longitude: invisible now, but it decides what happens later.
